title: Tic-tac-toe (N x N) and Chess outline
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, O(1) counter-based win check for N x N, extensibility, chess piece polymorphism outline, runnable Java and Kotlin, per-game locking, follow-ups.

Scope: requirements, O(1) counter-based win check for N x N, extensibility, chess piece polymorphism outline, runnable Java and Kotlin, per-game locking, follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design Tic-tac-toe for an N x N board where N in a row wins, then sketch how Chess extends the same ideas.

Functional:

  • Two players alternate; X starts.
  • A move is a (row, column) on an empty cell. Invalid moves are rejected and do not change the turn.
  • Win: a full row, column, or either diagonal of one player. Draw: board full with no winner.
  • Must work for any N (3, 5, 19 as in Gomoku with a different rule).

Non-functional: win detection should not scan the whole board on each move; the win rule should be extensible.

Worked example. On a 3x3 board X plays (0,0), (0,1), (0,2). The row-0 counter for X goes 1, 2, 3 = N, so X wins after 3 moves with O's 2 moves wasted. The naive way scans 3 rows + 3 columns + 2 diagonals (about 24 cells) each move; the counter way does 4 increments. On a 1000 x 1000 board that is 4 operations versus about 4,000 scans.

Industry examples. Counting instead of rescanning is the same trick used by Gomoku engines (incremental line counts) and by game-of-life style engines; the "only check lines through the last move" idea is standard in Connect Four implementations.

Everyday analogy. Keeping a tally on a scoreboard for each line instead of looking at the whole board after every move.

Common interview traps.

  • Scanning the whole board each move; it is O(N^2) when O(1) is possible.
  • Forgetting that the diagonals only matter when r == c or r + c == N-1.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• TicTacToe (game and board together at this size): grid, per-player counters rows[p][i], cols[p][i], diag[p], anti[p], move count, whose turn, over.
  • MoveResult: OK, WIN, DRAW, INVALID. A result enum avoids exceptions for normal "that cell is taken" input.
  • For Chess: Piece (abstract) with Rook, Knight etc., and ChessBoard.

Why counters. A player wins a row exactly when their count in that row reaches N. Because only one player can own a cell, two arrays of counters (one per player) are enough. Space is O(N) instead of scanning O(N^2).

Decision gravity. Counters are fast but tie the win rule to "N in a full line". If a later requirement says "5 in a row on a 19x19 board" (Gomoku) the counters no longer work and you switch to checking the four directions around the last move: still O(k), but the rewrite touches the core method. Hide it behind a WinRule interface if that is likely. Reversible if hidden, a rewrite if not.

Everyday analogy. A referee who ticks a box each time a row gets another mark instead of looking at all the squares.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a single counter array with +1 for X and -1 for O: that works for two players (a trick) but breaks for 3+ players.
  • Letting an invalid move switch the turn.

Common interview traps.

  • Pawn, king and en passant belong to the board or game rules (they need context); a Piece knowing only its own geometry cannot do them.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Polymorphism (Chess pieces). Each piece owns its movement shape; the board owns the shared rules (own piece capture, blocking, check). This is Strategy by inheritance. Alternative: one switch(pieceType) in the board, which breaks open/closed when you add a fairy-chess piece.
  • Template Method (optional). The board's move is a fixed pipeline (turn check, shape, capture, path, apply) in which only canMove and slides vary.
  • Command (optional). Represent moves as objects (from, to, captured piece) to get undo and PGN logs.
  • Strategy for win rules if you generalise (N in a row on a bigger board).
  • State (optional). In progress, won, drawn.

Industry examples. Stockfish uses bitboards (a 64-bit integer per piece type) for speed; chess.com and Lichess store games as PGN/move lists, which is Command-like. Google's AlphaGo and Gomoku engines use incremental line counts as above.

Everyday analogy. A school with a rulebook for the playground (board rules) and each sport (piece) knowing only how its own ball moves.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting check detection inside Piece.
  • Starting to code all 6 pieces; in an interview do the structure, two pieces and describe the rest.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21). The chess part is an outline: two pieces plus the board pipeline, with a clear TODO for king safety.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

enum MoveResult { OK, WIN, DRAW, INVALID }

/** N x N board with O(1) win check: keep a running count per row, column and the two diagonals. */
class TicTacToe {
    protected final int n;
    protected final char[][] grid;
    protected final int[][] rows, cols;           // [player][index]; player is 0 or 1
    protected final int[] diag, anti;
    protected int moves = 0;
    protected int next = 0;                       // whose turn: 0 = X, 1 = O
    protected boolean over = false;
    private static final char[] SYMBOLS = {'X', 'O'};

    TicTacToe(int n) {
        this.n = n; grid = new char[n][n];
        rows = new int[2][n]; cols = new int[2][n]; diag = new int[2]; anti = new int[2];
    }

    MoveResult move(int player, int r, int c) {
        if (over || player != next || r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= n || c >= n || grid[r][c] != 0)
            return MoveResult.INVALID;
        grid[r][c] = SYMBOLS[player];
        moves++;
        boolean win = ++rows[player][r] == n | ++cols[player][c] == n;
        if (r == c && ++diag[player] == n) win = true;
        if (r + c == n - 1 && ++anti[player] == n) win = true;
        if (win) { over = true; return MoveResult.WIN; }
        if (moves == n * n) { over = true; return MoveResult.DRAW; }
        next = 1 - next;
        return MoveResult.OK;
    }
}

/* ---- Chess outline: shows how pieces plug in via polymorphism ---- */
abstract class Piece {
    final boolean white;
    Piece(boolean white) { this.white = white; }
    /** Shape rule only. The board adds: own-piece capture, path blocking, king safety. */
    abstract boolean canMove(int fr, int fc, int tr, int tc);
    boolean slides() { return false; }            // rook, bishop, queen slide; knight jumps
}
class Rook extends Piece {
    Rook(boolean w) { super(w); }
    boolean canMove(int fr, int fc, int tr, int tc) { return (fr == tr) != (fc == tc); }
    boolean slides() { return true; }
}
class Knight extends Piece {
    Knight(boolean w) { super(w); }
    boolean canMove(int fr, int fc, int tr, int tc) {
        int dr = Math.abs(fr - tr), dc = Math.abs(fc - tc);
        return dr * dc == 2;                      // (1,2) or (2,1)
    }
}
class ChessBoard {
    final Piece[][] sq = new Piece[8][8];
    boolean whiteToMove = true;

    boolean move(int fr, int fc, int tr, int tc) {
        Piece p = sq[fr][fc];
        if (p == null || p.white != whiteToMove || !p.canMove(fr, fc, tr, tc)) return false;
        if (sq[tr][tc] != null && sq[tr][tc].white == p.white) return false;   // own piece
        if (p.slides() && !pathClear(fr, fc, tr, tc)) return false;
        sq[tr][tc] = p; sq[fr][fc] = null; whiteToMove = !whiteToMove;
        return true;                              // TODO in a full engine: reject if own king is in check
    }
    private boolean pathClear(int fr, int fc, int tr, int tc) {
        int dr = Integer.signum(tr - fr), dc = Integer.signum(tc - fc);
        for (int r = fr + dr, c = fc + dc; r != tr || c != tc; r += dr, c += dc)
            if (sq[r][c] != null) return false;
        return true;
    }
}

Kotlin core of Tic-tac-toe (hand translated, not compiled in this session):

enum class MoveResult { OK, WIN, DRAW, INVALID }

class TicTacToe(private val n: Int) {
    private val grid = Array(n) { CharArray(n) }
    private val rows = Array(2) { IntArray(n) }
    private val cols = Array(2) { IntArray(n) }
    private val diag = IntArray(2)
    private val anti = IntArray(2)
    private var moves = 0
    private var next = 0
    private var over = false

    @Synchronized
    fun move(player: Int, r: Int, c: Int): MoveResult {
        if (over || player != next || r !in 0 until n || c !in 0 until n || grid[r][c] != '\u0000')
            return MoveResult.INVALID
        grid[r][c] = if (player == 0) 'X' else 'O'
        moves++
        var win = (++rows[player][r] == n)
        if (++cols[player][c] == n) win = true            // always run every increment
        if (r == c && ++diag[player] == n) win = true
        if (r + c == n - 1 && ++anti[player] == n) win = true
        if (win) { over = true; return MoveResult.WIN }
        if (moves == n * n) { over = true; return MoveResult.DRAW }
        next = 1 - next
        return MoveResult.OK
    }
}

Choices: | (not ||) is used in the win expression so both counters are always incremented. Here it is harmless either way, because a win ends the game and the skipped counter is never read again; it would matter only if counters were updated before the move was validated or the game continued after a win. A turn only switches on an OK result.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating counters before validating the move, or letting play continue after a win: then a short-circuited || that skips a counter update becomes a real, subtle bug.
  • Rook rule (fr == tr) != (fc == tc) means exactly one coordinate changes; || would allow a zero move.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        TicTacToe g = new TicTacToe(3);
        int[][] script = {{0,0},{1,0},{0,1},{1,1},{0,2}};   // X: row 0 ; O: wasted
        MoveResult last = null;
        for (int i = 0; i < script.length; i++) last = g.move(i % 2, script[i][0], script[i][1]);
        System.out.println("3x3 result = " + last);                        // WIN
        System.out.println("move after end = " + g.move(1, 2, 2));         // INVALID

        TicTacToe big = new TicTacToe(5);
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { big.move(0, i, i); if (i < 4) big.move(1, i, (i + 1)); }
        System.out.println("5x5 diagonal = " + big.over);                  // true

        ChessBoard cb = new ChessBoard();
        cb.sq[0][0] = new Rook(true); cb.sq[0][3] = new Knight(true); cb.sq[7][7] = new Rook(false);
        System.out.println("rook blocked = " + cb.move(0, 0, 0, 5));       // false (knight in the way)
        System.out.println("knight jump  = " + cb.move(0, 3, 2, 4));       // true

        SafeTicTacToe s = new SafeTicTacToe(3);
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        Future<MoveResult> a = ex.submit(() -> s.move(0, 1, 1));
        Future<MoveResult> b = ex.submit(() -> s.move(0, 1, 1));           // same player, same cell
        long ok = Stream.of(a.get(), b.get()).filter(r -> r == MoveResult.OK).count();
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("accepted moves = " + ok);                      // 1
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

3x3 result = WIN
move after end = INVALID
5x5 diagonal = true
rook blocked = false
knight jump  = true
accepted moves = 1

Covered: win, move after end, a 5x5 diagonal, chess rook blocked by a knight and a legal knight jump, and a concurrent duplicate move.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing the draw and diagonal paths.
  • Not testing that a rejected move leaves the turn unchanged.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Online play: two players' requests arrive on different threads. move reads the turn, checks the cell, writes the cell, updates counters and flips the turn. Interleaved, both threads may see the cell empty and both write it, or both see "my turn".

Fix: one lock per game around move, as the whole check-update-switch is a single logical step. Cost is negligible (a few microseconds of work).

class SafeTicTacToe extends TicTacToe {
    SafeTicTacToe(int n) { super(n); }
    // check turn + cell + counters + switch turn: one atomic unit, so a whole-method lock is right here
    @Override synchronized MoveResult move(int player, int r, int c) { return super.move(player, r, c); }
}

Gravity. For a game server with millions of games, the lock lives inside each game object; scale by routing a game id to one server (so the lock stays in-process), or by storing the game in Redis and using optimistic concurrency (a version number with compare-and-set; the loser retries or is rejected). An in-memory lock does not help once two servers hold the same game, which is the cross-server version of the same race.

Symptom in production. Two marks in one cell, or both players move twice. The metric: moves recorded per game greater than the cells filled.

Everyday analogy. Two people tapping the same square on one phone at the same instant: the screen must accept only the first tap.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking the board but not the turn variable.
  • Declaring the fields volatile and calling it safe; volatile does not make check-then-act atomic.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Gomoku (k in a row on a big board). Replace the counters with a check of 4 directions around the last move.
  • Undo. Keep a move stack (Command); undo decrements the counters.
  • AI opponent. Minimax with alpha-beta pruning; for 3x3 the full tree is under 400,000 positions. For bigger N use heuristics or Monte Carlo search.
  • 3+ players. Counters are per player already; only the turn rotation changes.
  • Full chess. Add Bishop, Queen, King, Pawn; castling, en passant and promotion in the board; check, checkmate and stalemate by trying each move and testing the king's square (legal-move generation).
  • Persistence and spectators. Event log of moves plus a pub/sub feed.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing minimax is exponential and needs pruning.
  • Forgetting that in chess a move that leaves your own king in check is illegal.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Tic-tac-toe NxN: per-player counters for each row, column and two diagonals give O(1) win detection; move result enum instead of exceptions.
  • Hide the win rule behind an interface if you may need k-in-a-row.
  • Chess outline: abstract Piece owns its shape, the board owns blocking, captures, turn and king safety.
  • Concurrency: one lock per game around the full check-update-switch; across servers use optimistic versioning or sticky routing.
  • Extensions: undo (Command), AI (minimax), Gomoku rule, full chess rules.

questions.promptHtml: How do you detect a win on an N x N tic-tac-toe board in O(1) per move, and why does it work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic "do not rescan the board" optimisation; tests whether you can keep running state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a count per player for each row, each column and the two diagonals. A move increments at most four counters (its row, its column, the main diagonal if r == c, the anti-diagonal if r + c == N-1). A player wins when any counter reaches N. A cell has one owner, so per-player counters never mix. That is O(1) time and O(N) space instead of scanning O(N^2).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
rows[p][r]++  cols[p][c]++  (r==c) diag[p]++  (r+c==n-1) anti[p]++
win if any of those == n

Worked example on 3x3: X plays (0,0), (0,1), (0,2): rows[X][0] goes 1, 2, 3 = N so X wins on the third move. On a 1000 x 1000 board, 4 increments versus about 4,000 scans. Return a MoveResult enum (OK, WIN, DRAW, INVALID) so a taken cell is a normal result, not an exception. A rejected move must not change the turn.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scanning the whole board after every move.
  • A single counter array with +1 for X and -1 for O: works for two players but breaks for three or more.
  • Letting an invalid move switch the turn.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why only check diagonals when r == c or r + c == n-1? -> Only cells on those lines belong to them.
  2. How do you detect a draw? -> Move count equals N x N with no winner.
  3. What if the rule becomes 5 in a row on 19 x 19? -> Counters no longer fit; check four directions around the last move.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "check row, column, diagonals". Senior: O(1) counters, why per-player, the draw rule, and the limits of the technique.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Incremental line counts are used in Gomoku and Connect-style engines for the same reason: rescanning dominates the cost.

questions.promptHtml: In a chess design, what belongs in the Piece classes and what belongs to the board or game? Why is a switch (pieceType) in the board a problem?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The chess outline question checks responsibility placement and open/closed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each piece owns its movement shape (canMove(from, to)) and whether it slides. The board owns everything that needs context: turn, capture of own piece, blocking along a path, check, castling, en passant, promotion. A switch on type in the board breaks open/closed: adding a new piece edits the board. Polymorphism is Strategy by inheritance, and the board's move is a fixed pipeline where only the shape varies.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Right turn? -> Piece shape ok? -> Not own piece? -> Path clear? -> Apply move (-> king safety)

A pawn cannot be fully expressed as a shape: forward moves differ from captures, the first move can be two squares, en passant needs the previous move. Those go in the board or a rules object. Check detection must not be inside Piece, because it needs the whole position. Interview approach: structure, two pieces (rook, knight), and a description of the rest.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting check detection in Piece.
  • Coding all 6 pieces instead of the structure.
  • A rook rule written with || which allows a zero move: use (fr == tr) != (fc == tc).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the knight not need pathClear? -> It jumps; slides() is false.
  2. How do you model undo and a game log? -> Command: a move object with from, to and captured piece.
  3. How does an engine represent the board for speed? -> Bitboards, one 64-bit integer per piece type (as in Stockfish).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "class per piece". Senior: splits shape from context rules, names Template Method for the pipeline, and says where pawns and king safety live.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Chess sites store games as move lists (PGN), which maps to Command objects and replay.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report that X sometimes wins with two marks on a 3x3 board, and that clicking a taken cell "costs" the player their turn. The code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
MoveResult move(int player, int r, int c) {
    boolean win = ++rows[player][r] == n | ++cols[player][c] == n;     // counters first
    if (r == c && ++diag[player] == n) win = true;
    if (r + c == n - 1 && ++anti[player] == n) win = true;
    if (over || player != next || grid[r][c] != 0) { next = 1 - next; return MoveResult.INVALID; }
    grid[r][c] = SYMBOLS[player];
    moves++;
    if (win) { over = true; return MoveResult.WIN; }
    next = 1 - next;
    return MoveResult.OK;
}
fun move(player: Int, r: Int, c: Int): MoveResult {
    var win = (++rows[player][r] == n) or (++cols[player][c] == n)     // counters first
    if (r == c && ++diag[player] == n) win = true
    if (r + c == n - 1 && ++anti[player] == n) win = true
    if (over || player != next || grid[r][c] != '\u0000') { next = 1 - next; return MoveResult.INVALID }
    grid[r][c] = if (player == 0) 'X' else 'O'
    moves++
    if (win) { over = true; return MoveResult.WIN }
    next = 1 - next
    return MoveResult.OK
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug and give the corrected order of operations.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices the turn flip but not that the counters were already changed by the rejected move.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should a rejected move change anything at all? Is the bounds check 0 <= r,c < n expected from this method?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reorder the method so validation is first and nothing changes on INVALID.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Counters incremented before validation: playing the same taken cell twice adds to the counters, so X "wins" with two cells on a 3x3 once the counter hits 3. (b) An invalid move flips next, so the turn is lost. (c) No bounds check, so grid[r][c] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds instead of returning INVALID.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests: same cell three times by the player to move; invalid move then valid move by the same player; out-of-range coordinates.
  5. Root cause: Validate-then-commit rule violated.
  6. Fix: First if (over || player != next || r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= n || c >= n || grid[r][c] != 0) return INVALID; with no side effects, then place the mark, then update counters, then decide win, draw, or switch turn.
  7. Prevention: A test asserting the full state (grid, counters, next) is unchanged after INVALID.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not throw exceptions for a taken cell: it is normal input, and MoveResult is cheaper. Note on the | operator: when a row win occurs the game ends anyway, so a skipped column counter does no harm today; | is still the safer style if undo or analytics later reads the counters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the first player check player != next inside the move? -> The server must not trust the client to say whose turn it is.
  • Does | versus || matter here? -> Only after a win, and the game is over; it matters if counters are used after the end.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A board game accepted clicks on an occupied cell and incremented the tally; a game was won with fewer marks than needed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes the turn flip only.
  • Hire: validate first with no side effects, adds bounds check.
  • Strong hire: full-state-unchanged tests and a calm view of the | versus || question.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a Gomoku mode: 19 x 19 board, first to get 5 in a row (horizontal, vertical or either diagonal) wins, anywhere on the board. The same codebase should still run 3x3 tic-tac-toe.
questions.promptHtml: Why do the counters stop working, what replaces them, and which classes change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps row counters and checks == 5, which counts marks in a row that are not consecutive.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exactly 5 or 5 or more? Are overlines allowed? Any opening restrictions? Two or more players?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; add a rule abstraction.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A row counter counts marks, not consecutive marks: X at columns 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 has count 5 and no run. So the win rule must examine adjacency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests: five non-adjacent marks do not win; five adjacent in each direction win; a run of 4 plus a gap does not.
  5. Root cause: Counters assumed "N cells in a full line".
  6. Fix: Interface WinRule { boolean wins(grid, r, c, symbol) }. FullLineRule keeps the counter approach for NxN. KInARowRule(k) counts consecutive marks in 4 directions through the last move:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean wins(char[][] g, int r, int c, char s) {
    int[][] dirs = {{0,1},{1,0},{1,1},{1,-1}};
    for (int[] d : dirs) {
        int run = 1 + count(g, r, c, d[0], d[1], s) + count(g, r, c, -d[0], -d[1], s);
        if (run >= k) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
fun wins(g: Array<CharArray>, r: Int, c: Int, s: Char): Boolean =
    listOf(0 to 1, 1 to 0, 1 to 1, 1 to -1).any { (dr, dc) ->
        1 + count(g, r, c, dr, dc, s) + count(g, r, c, -dr, -dc, s) >= k
    }

count walks while in bounds and equal to s. TicTacToe takes the rule by constructor; the move pipeline (validate, place, rule, draw, turn) is unchanged. 7. Prevention: Table tests for each direction and the gap case. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The k-run check is O(k) per move, still tiny. I would not keep both counters and the rule check; pick one per mode.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Exactly five" rules? -> Check run == k and forbid longer runs in that variant.
  • AI opponent? -> Minimax with alpha-beta; the full 3x3 tree is under 400,000 positions, 19x19 needs heuristics or Monte Carlo search.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A Gomoku clone reused row counters and declared wins from scattered stones; the bug surfaced in the first tournament.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reuses counters with 5.
  • Hire: four-direction run check behind a rule interface.
  • Strong hire: gap tests, overline rule question, minimax scale awareness.

questions.contextHtml: An intern's version uses one counter array with +1 for X and -1 for O and declares a win when abs(counter) == n. It passes all 2-player tests. The game is extended to three players (X, O, Z) on a 5x5 board with 4 in a line (full-row, not required).
questions.promptHtml: Why does the single-array trick break, and what is the right structure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds +2 for the third player.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the win "n in a full line" or a k-run? Order of players fixed? Can a draw be declared early?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block three-player games until fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The trick relies on +1 and -1 cancelling when both players are in the same line; with three players there is no encoding where mixed lines never reach n in absolute value. Also, with the trick you cannot tell who won without extra state.
  4. How I'd verify each: Counter-example: with X=+1, O=-1, Z=+2 a line of X, X, Z gives +4 with n = 4: a false win.
  5. Root cause: A clever encoding that only works for exactly two players.
  6. Fix: Per-player arrays rows[p][i], cols[p][i], diag[p], anti[p] where p ranges over the player count, as the notes' structure already supports; only the turn rotation next = (next + 1) % players changes.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
rows = new int[players][n]; cols = new int[players][n];
diag = new int[players]; anti = new int[players];
next = (next + 1) % players;
rows = Array(players) { IntArray(n) }; cols = Array(players) { IntArray(n) }
diag = IntArray(players); anti = IntArray(players)
next = (next + 1) % players
  1. Prevention: Tests with 3 players where mixed lines reach but never win.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-player arrays cost O(players x N) space, negligible. I would not keep the two-player trick as an optimisation: it saves a few bytes at the price of a rewrite.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory for N = 1000, 4 players? -> 4 x (2 x 1000 + 2) ints, about 32 KB; the grid dominates at 1 million cells.
  • Why is the trick tempting? -> It halves the counters and the win check is one abs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A clever encoding in a prototype survived to production and blocked a multi-player mode until a rewrite.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adjusts the numeric encoding.
  • Hire: per-player counters, rotation changes.
  • Strong hire: constructs the counter-example and states the space cost.

questions.contextHtml:
ChessBoard.move is a 300-line switch (piece.type) with ROOK, KNIGHT, BISHOP... and each case duplicates the own-piece capture check. A game-variant team wants an "Amazon" piece (queen plus knight moves) and a "Nightrider". Each addition touches the same method and has twice broken the rook.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
switch (p.type) {
    case ROOK:   ok = (fr == tr) != (fc == tc) && pathClear(fr, fc, tr, tc); break;
    case KNIGHT: ok = Math.abs(fr - tr) * Math.abs(fc - tc) == 2; break;
    // ... 300 lines
}
val ok = when (p.type) {
    PieceType.ROOK -> (fr == tr) != (fc == tc) && pathClear(fr, fc, tr, tc)
    PieceType.KNIGHT -> abs(fr - tr) * abs(fc - tc) == 2
    // ... 300 lines
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor, name the pattern, and explain where the shared rules go.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Splits the switch into private methods per piece but keeps the switch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which rules need board context (pawn, castling, check)? Are variants chosen at game start? Any piece-specific data such as "has moved" (needed for castling)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin existing behaviour with tests per piece before touching the code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Variation by type is the cue for polymorphism: Strategy by inheritance. Shared pipeline is Template Method.
  4. How I'd verify each: Move tables per piece (all legal and illegal squares from a given square on an empty board) run against old and new code.
  5. Root cause: Open/closed violation: every new piece edits the board.
  6. Fix: abstract class Piece { abstract boolean canMove(...); boolean slides() }, subclasses Rook, Knight, Amazon (queen shape or knight shape), Nightrider (repeated knight steps, so it also needs a custom path check). The board's move is the pipeline: right turn, shape, not own piece, path clear (for sliders), apply, then king safety. Pawn, castling and en passant stay in the board or a rules object because they need context.
  7. Prevention: A test per piece with an expected move table; new pieces add a new table, no existing test changes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More classes and virtual calls; irrelevant at this scale. A real engine uses bitboards for speed, not objects, so I would say that rather than optimise now. I would not put check detection in Piece.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Nightrider slides along knight steps, so pathClear as written is wrong. -> Override a path(from, to) method on the piece so the board asks the piece which squares it crosses.
  • Who stores "has moved"? -> A field on the piece or a set on the board; the board needs it for castling.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Adding a variant piece to a monolithic switch broke castling because two cases shared a local variable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: private method split.
  • Hire: polymorphic Piece, board pipeline, tests first.
  • Strong hire: notices the Nightrider path problem, places contextual rules correctly, mentions bitboards for real engines.

questions.contextHtml:
In online play, support shows a game with two marks in one cell and an alert "moves recorded 11 > cells filled 9" on a 3x3 board. Logs:

09:15:02.331 g-9 node=app-1 move(p0, 1, 1) -> OK    (version 4)
09:15:02.333 g-9 node=app-2 move(p0, 1, 1) -> OK    (version 4)
09:15:02.700 g-9 client retry move(p0, 1, 1) after timeout -> INVALID (cell taken)

The game object has a synchronized move. The service runs 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer and loads the game from Redis per request, then saves it.
questions.promptHtml: Why does synchronized not help, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized to move" (already there) or "use a bigger lock".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is game state loaded per request? Does the client send a move id? Can requests for one game be routed to one node?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Sticky routing by game id at the load balancer, which makes the in-process lock meaningful again.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two nodes loaded the same version 4, each applied a valid move in its own JVM memory, both saved. The lock is per object per JVM, so it cannot span nodes. Retry returning INVALID is the correct behaviour on a duplicate; the real bug is the lost update.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare versions in the logs (both at version 4); count moves per game vs filled cells.
  5. Root cause: Cross-process check-then-act without a version check on save.
  6. Fix: Optimistic concurrency: every game has a version; the save is a compare-and-set (SET game IF version = 4 as a Lua script or a DB UPDATE ... WHERE version = 4); the loser reloads and the move re-validates (now INVALID) or is rejected. Add an idempotency key per move so a client retry after a timeout returns the original result.
  7. Prevention: The moves > filled invariant as an alert; a two-client test against the real store.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sticky routing is simple but breaks on node failover; optimistic CAS works anywhere at the cost of a retry on conflicts, which are rare in a two-player game. I would not use a distributed lock as the default: lease expiry and clock issues, and CAS needs no lock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why volatile fields do not help? -> They give visibility, not atomic check-then-act, and not across JVMs.
  • What does the loser see? -> A "conflict" result and the latest state, so the UI can refresh.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A board game service scaled from one pod to four and the "impossible" double move appeared within a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more synchronized.
  • Hire: identifies cross-node scope and uses versioned CAS.
  • Strong hire: also gives sticky routing as a stopgap, idempotency and the invariant alert.

questions.contextHtml: You must complete the chess design: bishops, queen, king, pawn, castling, en passant, promotion, and rules for check, checkmate and stalemate. The current move only checks shape, own piece, and path, with a TODO for king safety. A reviewer says: "put isInCheck() on King and let the board ask the king."
questions.promptHtml: Where does legality live, how do you generate legal moves, and what are the traps?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Follows the reviewer, so the king checks attackers by itself and cannot see pinned or blocked lines properly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this for human play only or an engine? Do we need PGN logs and undo? Are draw rules needed (repetition, 50 move)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; scoping the work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: King safety needs the whole position (all enemy pieces and blockers), so it belongs to the board or a rules object, not to a single piece.
  4. How I'd verify each: Known positions with known legal move counts (perft-style tests: count the moves to a given depth and compare with published values; verify the numbers from a reference).
  5. Root cause (design): Context-dependent rules do not belong to a context-free piece.
  6. Fix: Pseudo-legal generation: each piece produces shape moves (canMove + path). Legal filter: apply the move as a Move command (from, to, captured, flags), test whether the mover's king square is attacked, undo. Castling requires: king and rook unmoved, squares between empty, king not in check and not passing through or into attacked squares. En passant needs the previous move; promotion is a move flag. Checkmate means in check and no legal move; stalemate means not in check and no legal move. Command objects give undo for the make/unmake loop and a game log.
  7. Prevention: Perft tests, tests for pins (a pinned piece cannot move off the line), castling through check, en passant exposing the king.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Try-and-undo for every candidate is simple and robust (roughly 30 to 40 candidates per position, verify for your case), and fast enough for human play; an engine needs bitboards and incremental attack maps. I would not implement all six pieces' details in an interview: structure plus two pieces plus a clear description of the filter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you avoid copying the board on every try? -> Make/unmake with the Command object, restoring the captured piece and flags.
  • Three-fold repetition? -> Store position hashes (Zobrist keys) in a counter per game.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hobby engine let a pinned bishop move because king safety was only checked after the move for the moved piece's own line.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees with King.isInCheck().
  • Hire: board-level legality filter with make and unmake.
  • Strong hire: castling and en passant conditions, perft testing, honest scope for an interview.
